description: Press the scale with one thumb again, but now we audit the anchor properly: what your kilograms predict about every hang, carry and climb you own. Here is how to read your thumb press like a coach, and the steady-hold month that builds a lock your whole hand can trust.

lines: Today the kilograms get graded properly.
beats.title: THE ANCHOR AUDIT

beats.text: PAD FLAT, SLOW LEAN, TRUE PEAK

scenes.narration: Back to the bathroom scale. Kneel, thumb pad flat in the center, arm straight above it, and lean in slowly until the number peaks and holds for a full second. That is your press. Do the other thumb. Write both numbers down. Last time we met this test, we opened the engine room and looked at the nine muscles that run your thumb. Today is not about anatomy. Today the kilograms get audited, because your thumb press is the single best predictor hiding in this entire grip season: it forecasts how your hangs end, how your carries fail, and why some grips feel solid and others feel haunted. Got both numbers? Keep them. At the end of this video I will tell you exactly what they predict, and how to raise the one that matters.

lines: Your real score is the smaller number.
beats.title: THE WEAK THUMB RULE

scenes.label: PEAK THUMB PRESS, GRADED BY THE WEAK SIDE
scenes.narration: The lines, again: fifteen kilograms is trained, twenty-two is elite, under ten is untrained and fixable. But the audit rule stands above all three: your real score is your weaker thumb. Not the average. Not the good one. Every two-handed task in your life loads both anchors, and the effort ends when the first anchor lets go. A twenty-kilo right thumb standing next to a nine-kilo left is not a fifteen-kilo hand. It is a nine-kilo hand with a strong assistant. That sounds harsh until you see it as good news: the fastest way to raise your whole hand's grade is to raise the smaller number, and small numbers move fast. Hold both kilograms. Now let me show you the three places your thumb press is already silently grading you every week.
scenes.sub: under 10: untrained thumb - over 22: elite thumb engine

beats.text: THE HANG ENDS AT THE THUMB

lines: The thumb decides for how long.
beats.title: PREDICTION ONE: HANGS

beats.text: THE PEEL STARTS AT THE ANCHOR

scenes.narration: Prediction one: your hangs. Film a failing dead hang in slow motion and watch the order of events. The fingers do not simply open. First, the thumb, which wrapped over the fingers as their lock, starts to slide. The lock loosens, the fingers lose their backstop, and then the hand peels. The press you just measured is that lock's strength, read directly. A thumb that can drive fifteen-plus kilograms down through its pad can keep the lock pinned while the fingers endure. A nine-kilo thumb becomes the hang's expiry date no matter how heroic the fingers are. This is why some skinny guys out-hang bigger men with stronger fingers: the contest was never only fingers. It was fingers times anchor, and the anchor is a trainable thumb engine that most hang training never touches on purpose.

Prediction two: your carries. A farmer carry dies the same death as a hang, one hand at a time, and it is the thumb side that starts the peel when the handle begins to roll. Prediction three: your climbing and pulling. Every hard pull finishes with the thumb clamping down over the fingers or the hold, and the clamp force is your press, wearing work clothes. Three different tests, one shared ending, and one number that forecasts all of them. This is why hand specialists respect the thumb out of all proportion to its size, and why this channel keeps returning to it. Train the fingers and you raise three ceilings by a little. Train the anchor and you raise the floor under all of them at once. Your kilograms are not a party trick. They are the foundation measurement of the entire grip season, hidden inside the smallest test we do.

beats.text: THE ENGINE ROOM MUST FIRE TOGETHER
OWN THE NUMBER, DON'T VISIT IT

scenes.narration: Now the deep cut, the one that separates a real grade from a lucky one: steadiness. A press that spikes to seventeen and collapses is worth less, in every real grip, than a press that rises to fourteen and sits there like it pays rent. Real anchors do not visit their number; they live at it, second after second, while the fingers work. The shake in a press is the thumb's crew firing out of sequence, the small steering muscles arguing with the big cables. That argument is trainable, and it trains best exactly the way it is tested: slow leans, calm holds, numbers owned instead of grabbed. When you retest, score yourself twice: the peak, and the number you can hold steady for three full seconds. The second number is the honest one. Chase that one for a month and watch the peak quietly follow it upward, the way peaks always follow foundations.

beats.text: NO WEIGHT CLASS IN THIS TEST

scenes.narration: And the skinny note, one more time, because it is the best news in the season: this test has no weight classes and no bodyweight tax. The scale does not know what the rest of you weighs. A heavier rival brings no advantage to a thumb press except whatever training he has actually done, and almost nobody trains this. The field is level, the test is honest, and the engine responds to steady work within weeks. Skinny guys spend so long being told which tests are unfair to them. This is the one that was never unfair at all. It was just unmeasured. Now you have measured it.
Now press with me. Weak thumb today, seventy percent of your peak, hold it steady ten seconds. Calm, no shaking, no visiting. Own the number. Go.

Here is your month. Three press sessions a week, weak thumb first while it is fresh, five steady ten-second holds per side at seventy percent of peak, exactly like the block we just did. The weak side takes one extra hold until the two numbers meet. Between sessions, the thumb rests; its cables rebuild on the tendon schedule, not the motivation schedule. The mistake to retire is the spike: leaning in with your whole bodyweight hunting a lucky peak teaches the engine room to panic-fire, and panic does not hold bars. Replace it with the three-second rule. Every press you count, in training and in testing, must sit still for three seconds to count. If the base of your thumb aches deep during this block, reduce the lean, and see a professional if it persists. Foundations first. The peak is just the foundation's shadow, and it will move when the foundation does.

So, your anchor audit. Weak thumb under ten: you are not weak, you are unwired, and you have found the single highest-leverage number in your grip. Ten to fifteen with the gap closing: the foundation is being poured, keep the steady holds coming. Over twenty-two, steady for three seconds, both sides close: your thumb engine is elite, and your hangs, carries and climbs are all standing on an anchor most men never build. Whatever your numbers are, they are measurements of one trainable engine, not a grade on you. Drop both kilograms in the comments, weak side first, just the numbers. Retest in thirty days, same scale, three-second rule. Build the anchor, and the whole hand starts keeping its promises.

Same scale, both thumbs, thirty days from now: that is the retest. If this way of training makes sense to you, subscribe, because we test a new cable every episode. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Your Thumb Pinch Test Reveals Your Hidden Strength
